case_files.headline: Star Health, 2024: a data leak with a customer service bot
case_files.subject: Star Health customer data leak
case_files.description: Policy documents and medical reports belonging to Star Health customers were served on demand by Telegram chatbots, a leak distributed as a self-service product rather than a file.
case_files.vector: Not established publicly; the insurer confirmed unauthorised access and disputed the attacker's account of how the data was obtained

case_files.headline: National Public Data, 2024: a company you never used, holding everything about you
case_files.subject: National Public Data breach
case_files.description: A background-check broker most people had never heard of leaked a file advertised at 2.9 billion records, including Social Security numbers, then went bankrupt.
case_files.disclosed: Offered for sale April 2024; published broadly in August 2024
case_files.vector: Never fully established publicly; a sister site was separately found publishing a plaintext password file

case_files.headline: AT&T, 2024: who called whom, for nearly every customer
case_files.subject: AT&T call records breach
case_files.description: AT&T lost six months of call and text metadata for nearly all its mobile customers. Not what was said, who spoke to whom, how often, and from roughly where.
case_files.vector: A third-party cloud data warehouse account without multi-factor authentication
exposed: Cell site identifiers for some records

case_files.headline: Snowflake, 2024: 165 companies breached without anyone touching Snowflake
case_files.subject: Snowflake customer account compromises
case_files.description: Ticketmaster, AT&T, Santander and around 160 others lost data from their own cloud warehouses. The credentials came from infostealer malware, some of it years old.
case_files.vector: Credentials stolen by infostealer malware, used against cloud accounts that had no multi-factor authentication

case_files.headline: Change Healthcare, 2024: one login, and American healthcare stopped billing
case_files.subject: Change Healthcare ransomware attack
case_files.description: A remote access portal without multi-factor authentication let ransomware into the company that processes a third of American medical claims. 190 million people were in the data.
case_files.vector: Stolen credentials used on a Citrix remote access portal that had no multi-factor authentication

case_files.headline: The British Library, 2023: the ransom was refused and the catalogue stayed dark
case_files.subject: British Library ransomware attack
case_files.description: Rhysida exfiltrated around 600GB and auctioned it. The lasting damage was not the data leaving, it was that thirty years of accumulated systems could not simply be switched back on.
case_files.vector: Most likely compromised credentials for third-party access on a Terminal Services server provisioned without multi-factor authentication

case_files.headline: Okta, 2023: the breach arrived through the help desk, inside debugging files
case_files.subject: Okta customer support system breach
case_files.description: Attackers reached Okta's support case system and read HAR files customers had uploaded for troubleshooting. Those files contained live session tokens.
case_files.vector: A service account whose credentials had been saved into a personal Google profile on a managed device, used to access the customer support case management system and the HAR files stored in it
exposed: Session tokens and cookies in uploaded HAR files
Names and email addresses of support system users

case_files.headline: 23andMe, 2023: 14,000 accounts opened the door to 6.9 million people
case_files.subject: 23andMe credential stuffing breach
case_files.description: Attackers logged into 14,000 accounts with recycled passwords. A feature that connects relatives then exposed 6.9 million people who had done nothing wrong.
case_files.vector: Credential stuffing with passwords from earlier breaches, amplified by the DNA Relatives feature

case_files.headline: MGM Resorts, 2023: a ten-minute phone call to the help desk
case_files.subject: MGM Resorts cyberattack
case_files.description: Attackers found an MGM employee on LinkedIn, called the IT help desk pretending to be them, and got a password reset. Slot machines and room keys stopped working for ten days.
case_files.vector: Social engineering of the IT help desk to obtain a credential reset, then abuse of the identity provider
exposed: A smaller set of Social Security and passport numbers

case_files.headline: MOVEit, 2023: one file transfer product, 2,700 organisations
case_files.subject: MOVEit Transfer mass exploitation
case_files.description: A zero-day in a file transfer product let one criminal group steal data from thousands of organisations over a single weekend, most of which had never heard of it.
case_files.vector: A SQL injection zero-day (CVE-2023-34362) in Progress MOVEit Transfer
exposed: Social Security and national ID numbers
Health data, depending on the victim organisation

case_files.headline: Latitude Financial, 2023: a licence number from 2005, stolen in 2023
case_files.subject: Latitude Financial data breach
case_files.description: Around 7.9 million driver's licence numbers and 6.1 million older records, some dating to 2005, taken from a lender using credentials stolen from an employee.
case_files.vector: Employee login credentials stolen and used to access two service providers holding customer data

case_files.headline: LastPass, 2022: the vaults were stolen, and then attacked offline
case_files.subject: LastPass data breach
case_files.description: An engineer's home media server was the way into a password manager's cloud backups. Customer vaults were copied, and attackers have been cracking them ever since.
case_files.vector: A compromised developer account, then a vulnerability in third-party software on a senior engineer's home computer

case_files.headline: AIIMS Delhi, 2022: the hospital went back to paper, and the record stayed thin
case_files.subject: AIIMS Delhi ransomware attack
case_files.description: Ransomware took India's flagship public hospital offline for weeks. What was taken, whether a ransom was demanded, and who was responsible were never established publicly.
case_files.vector: Not established publicly; ransomware affecting servers hosting the hospital's e-hospital systems

case_files.headline: Medibank, 2022: the company said no, and the data went up anyway
case_files.subject: Medibank data breach
case_files.description: Medibank refused to pay the ransom. The attackers published 9.7 million customers' health claims data in tranches, organised to cause the most distress.
case_files.vector: Stolen credentials belonging to a third-party IT contractor, with no multi-factor authentication
exposed: Health claims data including procedures and diagnoses

case_files.headline: Optus, 2022: an API with no lock on it, and 9.8 million Australians
case_files.subject: Optus data breach
case_files.description: An internet-facing Optus API required no authentication at all. Anyone who found it could walk the customer database, including identity document numbers.
case_files.vector: An internet-facing API endpoint that required no authentication and allowed enumeration of customer records

case_files.headline: Uber, 2022: multi-factor authentication held, and then somebody sent a WhatsApp message
case_files.subject: Uber 2022 internal systems breach
case_files.description: A contractor's password was bought, their phone was buried in approval prompts, and a helpful message finished the job. The real prize was an admin credential sitting in a script.
case_files.vector: Stolen contractor credentials, multi-factor fatigue plus social engineering over WhatsApp, then hardcoded privileged credentials found in an internal PowerShell script

case_files.headline: 0ktapus, 2022: one text message, one hundred and thirty companies
case_files.subject: 0ktapus phishing campaign
case_files.description: A single SMS phishing campaign harvested credentials and one-time codes from employees at more than 130 companies. Cloudflare was targeted with the same messages and lost nothing.
case_files.vector: SMS phishing to employees, directing them to convincing fake single sign-on pages that relayed credentials and one-time codes in real time

case_files.headline: Twitter, 2022: an API that confirmed which account owned which email
case_files.subject: Twitter API data exposure
case_files.description: A bug let anyone submit an email address or phone number and be told which Twitter account it belonged to. For pseudonymous users, that is the whole threat model.
case_files.vector: An API flaw allowing an email address or phone number to be resolved to an account
exposed: The linked account handle and public profile data

case_files.headline: T-Mobile, 2021: an exposed router, and 76 million people who were mostly not customers
case_files.subject: T-Mobile data breach
case_files.description: An internet-exposed router led to a data centre and then to records on tens of millions of people, most of whom had only ever applied for service.
case_files.vector: An internet-exposed router, then lateral movement into a data centre
exposed: Account PINs for some prepaid customers

case_files.headline: Kaseya, 2021: the update arrived on schedule and encrypted 1,500 companies
case_files.subject: Kaseya VSA supply chain ransomware attack
case_files.description: REvil exploited zero-days in Kaseya's remote management server to push ransomware down the trusted update channel into roughly 1,500 downstream businesses.
case_files.vector: Authentication bypass and code injection in internet-facing Kaseya VSA servers, used to distribute a malicious agent update

case_files.headline: Air India, 2021: ten years of passengers, lost by a supplier
case_files.subject: Air India data breach
case_files.description: Air India lost 4.5 million passengers' data, including passport details going back a decade, because the company that runs its reservation platform was breached.
case_files.vector: Compromise of SITA Passenger Service System, a shared platform used by many airlines
exposed: Some payment card data, without CVV

case_files.headline: Colonial Pipeline, 2021: one leaked password, and the fuel stopped
case_files.subject: Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack
case_files.description: A disused VPN account with no second factor let ransomware into the company that supplies nearly half the US East Coast's fuel. The pipeline stopped for six days.
case_files.vector: A legacy VPN account with no multi-factor authentication, using a password found in a breach dump
exposed: Personal data of a small number of individuals

case_files.headline: Facebook, 2021: 533 million phone numbers that were never "hacked"
case_files.subject: Facebook 533 million record scrape
case_files.description: Facebook was right that nobody broke in. Attackers abused a feature working as designed to match hundreds of millions of phone numbers to real profiles.
case_files.disclosed: Data sold in 2020; published free in April 2021
case_files.vector: Abuse of the contact importer feature to match bulk phone numbers to profiles
exposed: Some email addresses and dates of birth

case_files.headline: MobiKwik, 2021: the breach that was denied while people searched their own KYC files
case_files.subject: MobiKwik alleged data leak
case_files.description: Data said to cover 99 million MobiKwik users was offered for sale with a portal where anyone could look themselves up. The company called the reports baseless. The RBI ordered an audit.
case_files.occurred: Reported from January 2021; the sale portal appeared in March 2021
case_files.disclosed: Never formally disclosed by the company
case_files.vector: Not established publicly
exposed: Alleged KYC documents including Aadhaar and PAN card images

case_files.headline: Accellion FTA, 2021: the rehearsal for MOVEit
case_files.subject: Accellion File Transfer Appliance breach
case_files.description: Attackers found zero-day flaws in a twenty-year-old file transfer appliance nearing end of life and used them to rob central banks, regulators and hospitals at once.
case_files.vector: Chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Accellion's File Transfer Appliance, a legacy product approaching end of life

case_files.headline: SolarWinds, 2020: 18,000 organisations installed the backdoor themselves
case_files.subject: SolarWinds supply chain attack
case_files.description: Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build system and shipped a backdoor inside a signed software update. Around 18,000 customers installed it. Fewer than 100 were the point.
case_files.vector: Malicious code inserted into the SolarWinds Orion build pipeline and distributed as a digitally signed update

case_files.headline: Clearview AI, 2020: three billion faces, scraped and sold
case_files.subject: Clearview AI facial recognition database
case_files.description: Clearview AI built a face search engine from three billion images scraped off the public web, sold it to police forces, and then had its client list stolen.
case_files.vector: Mass automated scraping of public social media and websites, plus a February 2020 breach of the company's own client list
exposed: Source URLs linking each face to its original profile
Clearview's own client list and search counts

case_files.headline: Capital One, 2019: a firewall misconfiguration and 106 million applicants
case_files.subject: Capital One data breach
case_files.description: A misconfigured web application firewall let an attacker ask the cloud for its own credentials, then read 106 million credit card applications out of storage.
case_files.vector: Server-side request forgery through a misconfigured web application firewall, reaching cloud instance metadata

case_files.headline: First American, 2019: 885 million documents behind a number you could count up
case_files.subject: First American Financial document exposure
case_files.description: Sixteen years of mortgage paperwork, bank details, Social Security numbers, wire receipts, sat behind sequential document IDs in a URL, with no login of any kind.
case_files.occurred: Documents were reachable from at least 2003 until May 2019
case_files.vector: Insecure direct object reference, changing a document number in the URL returned another customer's file, with no authentication required

case_files.headline: Collection #1, 2019: 773 million addresses, and nobody was breached
case_files.subject: Collection #1 credential aggregate
case_files.description: Collection #1 was not a hack. It was 87GB of everyone else's hacks, merged and deduplicated into a single file built for one purpose: automated login attempts.
case_files.vector: Aggregation of thousands of earlier breaches into one deduplicated combination list

case_files.headline: Marriott and Starwood, 2018: a breach that came with the acquisition
case_files.subject: Marriott Starwood guest reservation database breach
case_files.description: Marriott bought Starwood in 2016. The reservation database it acquired had already been compromised for two years, and nobody found out until 2018.
case_files.vector: Long-running compromise of the Starwood reservation system, present before the acquisition

case_files.headline: British Airways, 2018: twenty-two lines of JavaScript
case_files.subject: British Airways data breach
case_files.description: A small change to a script on the BA payment page sent card details to the attackers as customers typed them. It ran for fifteen days and cost the airline a £20 million fine.
case_files.vector: Malicious JavaScript injected into the payment page, a Magecart-style client-side skimmer

case_files.headline: SingHealth, 2018: 1.5 million patients, taken on the way to one of them
case_files.subject: SingHealth cyberattack
case_files.description: An advanced attacker spent months inside Singapore's largest health system, repeatedly and specifically seeking one patient's records. A million and a half others were taken en route.
case_files.occurred: Initial compromise around August 2017; bulk exfiltration 27 June – 4 July 2018
case_files.vector: A compromised front-end workstation, then lateral movement to a privileged account and queries against the electronic medical records database

case_files.headline: Cambridge Analytica, 2018: the breach that was not a breach
case_files.subject: Facebook and Cambridge Analytica data scandal
case_files.description: Data on 87 million Facebook users reached a political consultancy. Nothing was hacked. The platform handed it over through a documented feature working exactly as designed.
case_files.vector: Legitimate use of Facebook's Graph API by a third-party app, then onward transfer of the data in breach of platform terms
exposed: Some private messages for a small subset

case_files.headline: Aadhaar, 2018: what the reported exposures actually showed
case_files.subject: Aadhaar data exposure reports
case_files.description: Reports of Aadhaar data being sold and leaked through third-party systems were denied by the authority as breaches of its database. Both positions can be true, and that is the lesson.
case_files.vector: Reported unauthorised access via intermediaries, and third-party systems exposing Aadhaar numbers through unsecured interfaces
exposed: Addresses and other demographic details, as reported by journalists and researchers

case_files.headline: Uber, 2016: the breach that was paid to disappear
case_files.subject: Uber data breach and cover-up
case_files.description: Uber lost 57 million records, paid the attackers $100,000 through its bug bounty programme, called it a research payment, and said nothing for a year.
case_files.vector: Credentials found in a private code repository, used to reach cloud storage

case_files.headline: Equifax, 2017: 147 million people, one unpatched web form
case_files.subject: Equifax data breach
case_files.description: The Equifax breach exposed 147.9 million people. A patch had been available for two months, and an expired certificate meant nobody saw the data leaving for 76 days.
case_files.vector: Unpatched Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638) in a consumer dispute portal

case_files.headline: NotPetya, 2017: the update that cost ten billion dollars
case_files.subject: NotPetya cyberattack
case_files.description: A backdoored update to Ukrainian tax software destroyed the networks of shipping lines, drugmakers and food companies worldwide within hours. Damage is estimated at $10 billion.
case_files.vector: Compromised update server for M.E.Doc, Ukrainian tax accounting software, then automatic spread using EternalBlue and stolen credentials

case_files.headline: WannaCry, 2017: the patch had been available for two months
case_files.subject: WannaCry ransomware outbreak
case_files.description: A leaked intelligence-agency exploit turned ransomware into a worm that needed nobody to click anything. Microsoft had shipped the fix in March. The NHS lost 19,000 appointments in May.
case_files.vector: The EternalBlue exploit against Microsoft's SMBv1 file-sharing protocol, leaked publicly the previous month and patched by Microsoft in March 2017
exposed: Encrypted files across hospitals, manufacturers and logistics firms

case_files.headline: Yahoo, 2013–2014: three billion accounts, and three years of silence
case_files.subject: Yahoo data breaches
case_files.description: Yahoo lost every account it had, three billion of them, in two separate intrusions, then disclosed them three years later in the middle of selling the company.
case_files.disclosed: September and December 2016; revised to 3 billion in October 2017
case_files.vector: Spear-phishing an employee, then forged authentication cookies
exposed: Security questions and answers, some unencrypted

case_files.headline: Dropbox, 2012: an employee reused a password, and 68 million accounts followed
case_files.subject: Dropbox data breach
case_files.description: A Dropbox employee used their LinkedIn password on a corporate account. When LinkedIn was breached, so was Dropbox, 68 million credentials, revealed four years later.
case_files.disclosed: Confirmed at the time as an email exposure; full scale revealed August 2016
case_files.vector: An employee's password, stolen in the LinkedIn breach, reused on a corporate account
exposed: Password hashes, about half bcrypt, about half salted SHA-1

case_files.headline: MySpace, 2016: 360 million accounts from a website nobody used any more
case_files.subject: MySpace data breach
case_files.description: The MySpace passwords were years old and the site was long abandoned. That is exactly why the breach worked, abandoned accounts still hold passwords people reuse.
case_files.vector: Never publicly detailed; passwords stored as unsalted SHA-1 of the first ten characters, lowercased

case_files.headline: VTech, 2015: six million children in a toy company's database
case_files.subject: VTech data breach
case_files.description: A breach of a children's tablet maker exposed 6.4 million child profiles, along with chat logs and photographs. The attacker's stated motive was to prove it was possible.
case_files.vector: SQL injection against the Learning Lodge app store, with passwords protected only by unsalted MD5 and security answers stored in plain text
exposed: Password hashes and plain-text security answers
Chat logs and photographs from Kid Connect

case_files.headline: TalkTalk, 2015: a nineteen-year-old and a webpage nobody owned
case_files.subject: TalkTalk data breach
case_files.description: TalkTalk lost 156,959 customers' data to a SQL injection attack on three webpages it had inherited in an acquisition and forgotten about. Teenagers found them.
case_files.vector: SQL injection against legacy webpages inherited from the Tiscali UK acquisition
exposed: Bank account numbers and sort codes

case_files.headline: Ashley Madison, 2015: when the data itself was the weapon
case_files.subject: Ashley Madison data breach
case_files.description: The Impact Team did not sell the Ashley Madison data. They published it, 32 million people, a paid deletion service that did not delete, and consequences measured in lives.
case_files.vector: Never publicly established; the attackers claimed insider-level access
exposed: Partial card data and transaction records
bcrypt password hashes, plus a weak legacy token

case_files.headline: OPM, 2015: 21.5 million security clearance files, fingerprints included
case_files.subject: US Office of Personnel Management data breach
case_files.description: The US government lost the background investigation files of 21.5 million people, every relationship, debt and indiscretion disclosed to get a security clearance.
case_files.vector: Stolen contractor credentials, then malware providing persistent access
exposed: Drug use and arrests disclosed on clearance forms

case_files.headline: Anthem, 2015: 78.8 million health records and one query that looked wrong
case_files.subject: Anthem data breach
case_files.description: A database administrator noticed a query running under his own name that he had not run. Behind it were 78.8 million member records, taken over the course of a year.
case_files.vector: Spear-phishing a subsidiary, then stolen credentials into a data warehouse

case_files.headline: Sony Pictures, 2014: the breach that destroyed the computers on the way out
case_files.subject: Sony Pictures Entertainment hack
case_files.description: Attackers took everything a film studio had, emails, salaries, medical records, unreleased films, then wiped the machines and published the contents week by week.
case_files.vector: Not fully detailed publicly; the malware included a component that wiped drives

case_files.headline: JPMorgan Chase, 2014: one server without two-factor authentication
case_files.subject: JPMorgan Chase data breach
case_files.description: A bank spending a quarter of a billion dollars a year on security lost contact data for 83 million households because a single server had been missed in an upgrade.
case_files.vector: Stolen employee credentials used against a server that had not been upgraded to two-factor authentication

case_files.headline: Home Depot, 2014: 56 million cards through a supplier's login
case_files.subject: Home Depot data breach
case_files.description: Attackers used a third-party vendor's stolen credentials to reach Home Depot's network, then ran custom malware on self-checkout tills for five months.
case_files.vector: Stolen third-party vendor credentials, privilege escalation, then memory-scraping malware on self-checkout point-of-sale terminals

case_files.headline: eBay, 2014: 145 million users and a notice nobody saw
case_files.subject: eBay data breach
case_files.description: Attackers used a handful of employees' credentials to reach eBay's user database and sat inside for months. The company then handled the announcement about as badly as it could.
case_files.occurred: Late February – early March 2014, discovered in May
case_files.vector: Compromised credentials belonging to a small number of eBay employees, used to reach the internal network

case_files.headline: Morrisons, 2014: the auditor who published the payroll
case_files.subject: Morrisons payroll data leak
case_files.description: A senior internal auditor with a grudge copied the payroll file of nearly 100,000 Morrisons staff and posted it online. The case ran to the UK Supreme Court and changed employer liability.
case_files.vector: Abuse of authorised access by a senior internal auditor, exfiltrated on a personal USB drive

case_files.headline: Target, 2013: 40 million cards, and the air-conditioning contractor
case_files.subject: Target data breach
case_files.description: Attackers entered Target's network through a refrigeration contractor's stolen login, then scraped 40 million card numbers from the tills during the Christmas rush.
case_files.vector: Stolen credentials belonging to a refrigeration contractor, then memory-scraping malware on the tills

case_files.headline: Adobe, 2013: 153 million records and the world's worst crossword
case_files.subject: Adobe data breach
case_files.description: Adobe encrypted its passwords instead of hashing them, then stored every password hint in plain text beside them, turning the dump into a puzzle anyone could solve.
case_files.vector: Intrusion into internal systems; source code taken alongside customer data

case_files.headline: LinkedIn, 2012: 6.5 million hashes that turned into 165 million accounts
case_files.subject: LinkedIn data breach
case_files.description: LinkedIn stored passwords as unsalted SHA-1. Six and a half million hashes leaked in 2012; four years later the full 165 million-account file went on sale.
case_files.vector: Never fully detailed publicly; passwords stored as unsalted SHA-1

case_files.headline: PlayStation Network, 2011: 77 million accounts and 23 days offline
case_files.subject: PlayStation Network outage and data breach
case_files.description: Sony took PlayStation Network down for 23 days after attackers took 77 million account records. The ICO later found the attack could have been prevented.
case_files.vector: Intrusion into application servers running outdated, unpatched software behind an inadequately protected network boundary

case_files.headline: RockYou, 2009: the 32 million plaintext passwords that became a wordlist
case_files.subject: RockYou data breach
case_files.description: A widget company stored 32 million passwords in plain text and lost them to a basic SQL injection. The file became the wordlist the whole security industry still uses.
case_files.vector: SQL injection against an unpatched web application

case_files.headline: Heartland, 2008: 130 million cards from a company that had just passed its audit
case_files.subject: Heartland Payment Systems data breach
case_files.description: Heartland was certified compliant with the card industry security standard. A SQL injection flaw let attackers plant a sniffer on the network that processed 100 million transactions a month.
case_files.vector: SQL injection into a corporate web application, then lateral movement and a packet sniffer on the payment network

case_files.headline: TJX, 2007: the wireless network in the car park
case_files.subject: TJX Companies data breach
case_files.description: Attackers sat outside a Marshalls store, broke the shop's weak wireless encryption, and worked inwards until they reached the card processing systems.
case_files.vector: Weak WEP wireless encryption at a store, then lateral movement to card processing systems
exposed: Some driver's licence numbers and names
